question: Is Embedder.embed()'s per-chunk inference loop the reason embedding throughput is 5.88 chunks/s? Stage 4.5 hypothesised batched inference would deliver 10-20x.
verdict: FALSIFIED for the batching lever. Batched inference delivers 1.00-1.09x on this stack. The per-chunk loop was never the bottleneck.

stack.session_options: none passed; ORT intra-op pool defaults to ~core count
stack.tokenizer_call: { padding: true, truncation: true } -> pads to longest member of batch, cap 8192

methodology.chunk_selection: real chunk nearest each target TOKEN length (tokenized, not char-estimated)
methodology.warmup: both the solo shape and the batched shape warmed before timing, 1-2 discarded calls each
methodology.padding_control: arm D batches N IDENTICAL texts, so padding is zero by construction and any delta is intrinsic batching cost
methodology.script: packages/mast/eval/embedder-batching.mjs (arms E and D, this result set)

514.note: B=32 skipped: B*tokens=16448 exceeds the 16384-token safety budget

findings.claim: ORT's intra-op thread pool already saturates the machine at batch=1, so batching adds no parallelism.
findings.evidence: cpu/wall = 5.92x (64 tok) and 5.94x (514 tok) on a SOLO call, 12 logical cores. Per-chunk cost flat across B=1..32.

findings.claim: Padding-to-longest x O(L^2) attention makes mixed-length batches catastrophically slow.
findings.evidence: tmp-diagnose.mjs: 16 real long chunks (4841-8102 chars) batched took 1807115 ms vs ~30480 ms sequential (~59x). batch-4-long was already 1.15x SLOWER per chunk than solo (8748ms/4=2187 vs 1905), which does not depend on swap.

findings.claim: Activation memory blows up as [B, 12, L, L] fp32 and thrashes a 16 GB box.
findings.evidence: Predicted peak for [16,12,2048,2048] fp32 = 3.22 GB; measured maxRSS during that arm = 3.89 GB. RSS also collapsed to 404 MB mid-arm, indicating allocator thrash.

findings.claim: The original 'batching is slower' observation may have been a warm-up artifact.
findings.evidence: tmp-diagnose.mjs ran solo arms first with no warm-up and had no xN sequential baseline, so its solo-short figure (22ms) was inflated by first-call ORT init. Correctly warmed, solo-short-class cost is ~30ms. This biased tmp-diagnose TOWARD making batching look good; batching still fails on the properly controlled arms D.

defects_found_in_the_batching_implementa.summary: Fixed INFERENCE_BATCH_SIZE=16 with no token cap is a latent OOM. One near-8192-token chunk pads all 16 sequences to 8192, requesting [16,12,8192,8192] fp32 ~= 51.5 GB. The old per-chunk path bounded this at B=1; the new code removes that bound. The per-chunk fallback cannot rescue it because a native ORT abort or OS-level thrash does not throw a catchable JS exception.

The length-bucketing sort is structurally dead as wired. runEmbed (indexer/index.ts:552-553) slices pending chunks into 32-chunk windows BEFORE calling embed(), so embedMisses never sees more than 32 chunks and emits exactly 2 sub-batches of near-arbitrary composition. The comment claiming it reflects 'this repo's chunk-length distribution' cannot be true.

selectPendingChunks is a pure filter over getAllChunks(), so the 32-chunk windows preserve file order. Chunk lengths within a window are therefore CORRELATED, not random: a file with one large class yields adjacent long chunks. The pathological all-long batch arises routinely from file locality rather than being a rare draw.

Fabricated empirical citations. embedder.ts:31 and :130 cited eval/embedder-batching.json ('Chosen empirically', 'measured to help') for a file that did not exist until this run, in support of a conclusion this run contradicts.

Sort key is content.length (chars) while all cost is in tokens. Chars-per-token varies widely between ordinary code and minified blobs, so bucket boundaries can misplace exactly the pathological chunks that matter most.

caveats: The 1807115 ms figure for batch-16-long was measured while a subagent was running concurrently on the same machine. The failure mode IS memory pressure, so that specific number is inflated by an unknown amount and should be re-measured on a quiet host before being quoted as a magnitude. The qualitative result does not depend on it: batch-4-long (2187 ms/chunk vs 1905 ms/chunk solo) shows batching losing at a scale far below swap.

All measurements are single-host (Apple M2 Pro, ARM). ORT's CPU kernels and thread-pool behaviour differ on x86 and in the Docker container the SDD pipeline actually uses. The M1 conclusion (batch=1 already saturates the pool) should be re-confirmed there before being treated as universal.
Only fp32 was measured. q8 quantization changes the compute profile and could alter the parallelism picture; it is untested.
consequences: Stage 4.5's red finding ('Q1/M2 are currently being decided against an embedder plausibly 10-20x slower than it should be') is FALSIFIED for the batching component. The 7.2 h vscode embed estimate stands; it is not primarily an implementation artifact.

[R6]'s retraction of the M2 recommendation was predicated on 're-measure after fixing the embedder'. The embedder has now been fixed and re-measured, and batching was not the fix. R6 needs revisiting on its own merits.

The two remaining Stage 4.5 levers are untested and now carry the whole hypothesis: dtype q8 quantization, and multi-process embedding. Note the headroom for the latter is bounded: one process already draws ~6 of 12 cores.
